key_terms: Assigning a record to bucket h(k) mod P from a hash of its key k and a partition count P. The same key keeps its bucket only while the hash function, key encoding and partition count stay unchanged.
An uneven distribution in which one hot key or bucket receives far more records than the others, so the worker that owns it becomes the bottleneck.
Partial results, such as per-partition sums and counts, that can be combined in any order into the same final answer without recovering the source order.
Redistributing records across workers so that all records with the same grouping key meet. Its cost includes serialization, network transfer, buffering, file writes and scheduling barriers.

worked_examples.title: Bucket keys with a stable hash
worked_examples.code:
import hashlib
from collections import Counter


def bucket(key: str, partitions: int = 4) -> int:
    digest = hashlib.sha256(key.encode()).digest()
    return int.from_bytes(digest[:8], "big") % partitions


counts = Counter(bucket(f"customer-{n}") for n in range(200))
print(sorted(counts.items()))
print(bucket("customer-7") == bucket("customer-7"))
worked_examples.interpretation: The four bucket counts fall between 40 and 64 around an ideal of 50, which is ordinary variation for a good hash over only 200 distinct keys. The repeated call returns True on every run and every machine because SHA256 does not depend on a per-process seed, unlike the built-in Python hash for strings. Spread across distinct keys says nothing about load when one key dominates, which the next example shows.

worked_examples.title: Measure skew from one hot key
worked_examples.code:
import hashlib
from collections import Counter


def bucket(key: str, partitions: int = 4) -> int:
    digest = hashlib.sha256(key.encode()).digest()
    return int.from_bytes(digest[:8], "big") % partitions


events = ["hot"] * 180 + [f"k{n}" for n in range(20)]
plain = Counter(bucket(key) for key in events)
salted = Counter(bucket(f"{key}#{i % 4}") for i, key in enumerate(events))
print(max(plain.values()), max(salted.values()))
worked_examples.interpretation: Without salting, one bucket holds at least the 180 hot events, so one worker does most of the job while three idle. Salting spreads the hot key across sub-keys and the largest bucket shrinks sharply. The cost is a second step: per-salt partial results must be merged, and averages can be merged only from sums and counts, never from per-salt averages.

evidence: Complete actual local program with independent expected values and explicit negative checks; distributed-system claims are excluded.
